entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Communist Party of Vietnam (Đảng Cộng sản Việt Nam, CPV), founded 1930 by Hồ Chí Minh in Hong Kong with Comintern support, is the governing and only legal party of Vietnam — leading the country through French colonial resistance (1930-1954), division and reunification war (1954-1975), and post-war transformation from centrally planned to market-oriented economy (Đổi Mới reforms, 1986) that grew Vietnam into one of Asia's fastest-growing economies. The CPV's 'bamboo diplomacy' — flexible foreign policy maintaining autonomy from both China and the West — is considered a model for small-state diplomacy.

Hồ Chí Minh founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930, reorganized as the Vietnam Workers' Party (1951) and Communist Party of Vietnam (1976 following reunification). The Viet Minh — the CPV's wartime front — expelled French forces after the Battle of Điện Biên Phủ (1954), then resisted American intervention (1965-1973) and reunified Vietnam under communist rule in 1975 after the fall of Saigon.

The 1986 Đổi Mới ('renovation') reforms — launching a socialist-oriented market economy — transformed Vietnam from one of Asia's poorest countries to one of its fastest-growing: GDP growth averaging 6-7% annually for 30 years, extreme poverty falling from 58% (1993) to under 5% (2023). Vietnam maintains single-party control while pursuing economic liberalization — the CPV's 'bamboo diplomacy' maintains relations with the US (normalized 1995), Russia, and China simultaneously. Vietnam has 100 million people and is the world's largest exporter of cashews and second-largest of coffee.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Communist Party of Vietnam — defeating France at Điện Biên Phủ, defeating the US in the longest American war, and then launching Đổi Mới market reforms that lifted millions from poverty — achieved both the 20th century's most stunning military upset and one of its most successful economic transformations.
